lead: The photo comparison or flip test is a looksmaxxing practice in which a person compares photos of themselves with the mirror-reversed version of the same photo, or with their mirror reflection, to understand why they look different in pictures than in the mirror and to judge which version they look best in. People use it to assess symmetry, find their better side and choose which photos or angles present their face most favourably.

Related published research exists. In a 2010 Frontiers in Psychology study (Amestoy, Bouvard and Cazalets), about 71 percent of adults preferred the mirror image of their own face, while 76 to 84 percent preferred the standard orientation of a friend's face; the authors linked this to the mere-exposure hypothesis, since people mostly see themselves reversed in mirrors.[3] The effect was first reported in a 1977 study by Mita, Dermer and Knight.[3]

The mere-exposure effect, in which repeated exposure to a stimulus increases liking, was first studied by Zajonc in 1968,[1] and reference works describe facial symmetry as one factor in perceived attractiveness.[2]

chain: Compare a photo with its flipped copy or the mirror
Notice asymmetries and which orientation looks better
Choose better angles, photos and presentation
angle.text: The flip test helps people understand why they look different in photos than in the mirror, which is how others see them, and guides choices of angle, parting and grooming.

infobox: Mere-exposure effect, facial symmetry, mirror-image preference[1][2][3]

paras: A mirror shows a face reversed left to right, while a photo and other people see it the standard way. In the flip test, a person looks at a photo and its horizontally flipped copy side by side, or at both a mirror and a photo, and notes which looks better and where differences appear.

The mere-exposure effect holds that familiarity increases liking; Bornstein's 1989 meta-analysis of 208 experiments found r = 0.26.[1] Proponents of the flip test say people prefer their mirrored face because it is the one they see most.

Research directly tests this. A 1977 paper by Mita, Dermer and Knight, 'Reversed facial images and the mere-exposure hypothesis', is cited as finding that people preferred mirror-reversed versions of their own faces while close friends preferred the normal photographs.[3] The 2010 study by Amestoy and colleagues repeated the design in 38 adults and 72 children aged 3 to 12; preference patterns appeared in children from about 5 to 7 years, and a control group viewing unfamiliar faces showed no preference between orientations.[3]
Facial symmetry research is reported to link symmetry with perceived attractiveness, which is one reason communities compare original and flipped images.[2]
Community members use flips and side-by-side comparisons to evaluate symmetry, jaw and other features, and some say photos show how others see them.
No studies found of the flip test as a self-improvement practice. Related laboratory studies of mirror-image preference are described above.[3]

timeline.event: Zajonc begins studying the mere-exposure effect.[1]
Mita, Dermer and Knight report preference for mirror-reversed images of one's own face.[3]
Amestoy, Bouvard and Cazalets study the preference in children and adults.[3]

name: Photo comparison / flip test

card.summary: Comparing a face with its mirror image to judge looks; related to mere exposure, but the method itself is untested.
card.note: Perception differences are not clinically validated.

quick.overview:
The flip test means comparing your photo with a horizontally flipped copy, or with the mirror image, to see which looks better and how others may see you.

No published studies have tested the practice itself.
quick.mechanism: Believers say familiarity with the mirror image shapes preference; the mere-exposure effect is the related research.
quick.risks: No physical risks. Some community members report distress from close self-scrutiny, though this has not been studied here.
